source_thesis: Consecration means we are no longer our own, and we must keep ourselves free from binding engagements because we know not when the LORD may call.

One should readily and trustfully commit oneself and all that concerns one to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, accepting all things, whatsoever their cause, silently and with a tranquil mind as coming from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, rather than giving oneself up to vain and wandering thoughts which weary soul and body and waste time and strength.
We must make no account of the judgments of men, being glad when men esteem us not, since we belong to God and He disposes of our reputation.
Christian life is actual union with the Lord Jesus, who is in us as the life and source of all our experience and work, not merely a system or an imitation.
God hears the fevered heart that cries in silence and will not forsake the poor and needy; He turns the bitter pool into a bright and breezy lake.
In this conversation with God we are also employed in praising, adoring, and loving Him incessantly for His infinite goodness and perfection.
Mary is powerful against the devil: at the invocation of her name the demons flee, and recourse to her is the certain means of overcoming temptations, especially those of impurity.
Prayer is to be as simple, natural, and constant as a child asking a parent; God is a Father who delights to be sought for everyday needs, and prayer should not be hedged about with man-made rules.
The Kingdom of God develops gradually and requires individual labor; it is the business of the Saints, and it is the Kingdom of God or nothing.
The devil, who once was filled with joy by a Judas, is now humbled by a Judas, and threatens to incite another king to persecute the believer and turn him from the crucified King.
The name Adam represents the false supposition that Life is not eternal but has beginning and end, that the infinite enters the finite, and that Soul dwells in material sense.

The soul has free power to turn its will toward the Centre of Divine Life and Light or toward the Spirit of the World; when it has chosen, its free power ends, and its future joy or sorrow follows the choice.
True devotion to Mary consists in honoring her, invoking her, trusting in her intercession, and striving to imitate her virtues; it is not a license to sin but requires the intention to amend.
We must have the heart of a child, a will of wax, and a mind free from the slavery of affection, going boldly despite little stumblings while God holds us by our good-will.

We should not fear to live alone, since each hermit spirit dwells in its hidden sphere, and God alone feels our secret throbbings; the Lord who dwells on high knows all, yet loves us better than He knows.
A gift to build up the Kingdom is no proof of a true heart, since a person may give with an impure design.

A pastor owes his own soul's care first: regular self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are indispensably necessary, and charity cannot be kindled in others if it is extinguished in oneself.

A truly good will does all and is of more value than all; if the will is good, wholly conformed and united to God and guided by reason, it matters little that the flesh, the senses, and the exterior man incline to evil or that a man finds himself lacking in interior devotion, so long as he remains with his whole soul united to God by faith and a good will.
All property and gold and silver belong to the Lord; our legitimate business is to find out what the Lord wants done with what we possess and do it, whether to give all, one-tenth, or the surplus.
Angels pour blessing and joy without ceasing on each bud and blossom and sleeping bosom, pitying even wolves and tigers and receiving each mild spirit to inherit new worlds.
Avoid talking illness to the patient; make no unnecessary inquiries about symptoms and never speak aloud the name of the disease.
Believers should not lay up money as a fund for old age or future emergencies, but live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, making their only investment in His work and the poor.
Causality is not mere necessary connexion but Activity, known directly in our experience of volition; the only cause we know is a conscious rational will.
Christ in you is the hope of glory and the secret hid from ages; if Christ is in you, the 'I' goes and He becomes your purity, grace, and strength.

Christian Science commands mastery of the propensities: hold hatred in abeyance with kindness, conquer lust with chastity, revenge with charity, and deceit with honesty, choking these errors in their early stages.
Christianity claims to be a way of life for men whose nature involves both bodily and spiritual elements, and its sacramental principle provides for both, precluding unreal and negative spirituality.

Contemplation is not absence or laziness of will but great energy of will for love, in which the soul's energy is laid bare to God's energy and the two are closely united, entering unspeakable bliss and immensity of living.

Divine Love begins in us as a feeble flicker; God takes the will for the deed, and in time true love is given as a gift—the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost—when the wall dividing us from God goes down.
Earth is imprisoned by selfish, jealous fear that binds free love with bondage, and she calls to break this heavy chain so that spring's joy is not hidden.
Every Elder should have at least one trade, and if possible more than one, and the Saints should learn to be self-sustaining in practical arts.
Excessive grief for the dead is a want of faith and confidence in God, who is jealous of our hearts and will be loved without a rival.
Fear cannot evade as Love can pursue; the soul's fear of losing all beside God is overcome by a Love that out-pursues its evasions.
GOD's protection in danger is real, and we should commit ourselves to His keeping, finding His Word sweet in times of peril.
God fits the work to the worker and the worker to the work, providing both the needed individuals and the means when He orders something done for His glory.
God is all that is good, and the goodness that each thing hath is He; God doeth all-thing that is done, and sin is no deed and hath no substance.
God is the only Mind and the only power; to acknowledge any other power, such as matter, drugs, or mortal mind, is to dishonor God.
God the Father is a person with a habitation, shape, voice, and features, distinct from the Son, who is the express image of his person; both are together in one place in heaven.
God's eternity means his nature is without beginning or end, free from succession of time, and contains in itself the cause of time; time is in God rather than God in time.
God-consciousness has a principle of active contagion: often a human spark is wanted to ignite the spark in another, after which the Divine Fire springs up and grows without further human assistance.

He did not pray for relief but for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, finding it sweet to suffer with God; to enjoy the peace of paradise in this life we must accustom ourselves to familiar, humble, affectionate conversation with Him and watch that we neither do, say, nor think anything displeasing to Him.
Holy Thursday in Experience asks whether babes reduced to misery in a rich and fruitful land can sing a song of joy; where sun shines and rain falls, babe can never hunger there.
If God sometimes seems deaf to our cries, it is to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us.
If we take the MASTER's directions and assurances to His first disciples more fully as our guide, they are just as suited to our times as to those in which they were originally given.

In the Blessed Sacrament we often approach as receivers, but Christ said, 'Do this as a memorial of Me before God,' implying an act of giving; we should offer great love and thanks without regard to what we receive, and because first we give we then receive.
Instruct the sick that they are not helpless victims, for if they accept Truth they can resist disease and ward it off as positively as they can resist temptation to sin.
It is mental quackery to make disease a reality and then attempt its cure through Mind; one should efface from thought all forms and types of disease.

It is the stopping half-way that causes distress: living wholly worldly may bring contentment, living regenerated brings great joy, but trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings gloomy wretchedness, vacillation, and depression.
Just weights and measures, refusal of gifts and bribes by officials, and open access for the aggrieved are required to prevent injustices and oppressions of the poor.

Love and hatred must be together: if Love dwelt not in Trouble it could have nothing to love, and none could know what Love is if there were no Hatred, or what friendship is if there were no foe to contend with.
Man is not matter but the image and likeness of God, spiritual and perfect, incapable of sin, sickness, and death; mortals are counterfeits of immortals.

Marcion was not a Gnostic in the strict sense: he was guided by a soteriological interest, put all emphasis on faith rather than Gnosis, used neither Semitic religious wisdom nor Greek philosophy of religion, and never made a distinction between esoteric and exoteric religion.
Mary is the tower of ivory, the mystic neck through whom the life-giving graces flow from Christ the head into his mystical body, and no one receives grace except through her hands.
Mental malpractice is the injurious action of one mortal mind controlling another from wrong motives, and students must be taught to bar the door of thought against this seeming power.
Mortal life is a school of experience and a probation for proving ourselves worthy of exaltation; we are here to learn, improve, and increase, not to stand still.
Never pray for riches; those who do more than pray for daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life.
Nothing should be wasted; even a crust or kernel must be saved, and frugality with what God bestows preserves and increases blessings.

One way to recollect the mind easily in prayer and preserve tranquility is not to let it wander too far at other times, keeping it strictly in the presence of God so that frequent thinking of Him makes it easy to keep calm in prayer or recall it from wanderings.

Our part and righteousness is to obey and renounce our own will, accepting and abiding by the Will of God; this self-surrender is counted to us for sufficient righteousness, yet we remain conscious that we have no righteousness of our own, as one bathed in sunlight cannot say 'I am the sun.'
Perfect charity requires the avoidance of all deliberate venial sin; venial sins dispose the soul to mortal sin both naturally, by forming habits, and supernaturally, by the loss of additional grace.

Prayer brings spiritual strength—hearts comforted, that is, encouraged, strengthened, and consoled—and this is a supreme need for individuals and for churches, for with strong, courageous, cheerful hearts Christians can face anything.
Preachers should not teach what they do not understand; where the Lord has not revealed a doctrine, say so and do not give an unsafe interpretation.
Reading the word of God on one's knees, turning promises and precepts into prayer, is a means of grace that gives insight, self-searching, and the very language of prayer.
Riches or hoarded wealth would have been a snare and an obstacle to a life of self-denial based on scriptural principle, so voluntary poverty for the Lord's sake is to be embraced.
Secret prayer is indispensable: public prayer and converse with brethren cannot make up for closet communion, and the way to obtain a spirit of prayer is to continue praying.

Singleness of heart is the most necessary condition of faith and true virtue; we must return to the simplicity of little children, cutting off the inordinate affections of vice, to enter the kingdom of heaven.
Suffering is a mental condition; when an accident happens, declaring that you are not hurt and understanding why brings good effects in proportion to your fidelity to divine metaphysics.

The Anthropological Argument deserves chief place among the proofs of God's existence because it adds to causative power and contriving intelligence the wider ideas of personality and righteous lordship, assuring us of a personal Being who rules us in righteousness and is the proper object of supreme affection and service.
The Christian doctrine of sin rests on Christ's authority verified in moral experience, not on Genesis being literal history; the early chapters may be treated allegorically.

The Church is not a voluntary organisation nor merely a body for maintaining public worship, but the Body of Christ, the creation of God, whose worship is the breath of its life and whose service of the world is the business of its life.

The Church's divisions leave it powerless to bring home its appeal as the nation does; membership in the Church does not make men feel a personal obligation, and there is no realised bond of corporate unity among Christians.

The God-conscious life is not abnormal but the complete, full, and only truly normal life, bringing balance between soul and body, heart and mind, and a greatly magnified intelligence; if all attained it, this world would become Paradise.

The Incarnation is the predestined climax of creation and the reconsecration of the whole universe, not merely the remedy for sin; the religion of the Incarnation must not be narrowed into the religion of the Atonement.
The Lord requires one-tenth of the whole person—brain, heart, nerve, and bone—for building temples, the ministry, and caring for the poor.

The Muse who dreamed of gods, heroic Greece, nymphs, and the beauty of what seems is now all but dead before the ghastly, jarring Truth that questions all; she should be allowed to dream, for roused she would surely die.
The Revelator saw the human and divine coincidence shown in the man Jesus, as divinity embracing humanity in Life and its demonstration.
The Saviour cannot pass away, and with Him lives our joy; faith makes the vision of unseen glory plain and speeds our gaze beyond time and death.
The Word of Wisdom is like all the counsels of God, in force today as much as ever, with life everlasting in it for those who observe it.
The attributes of God are objective qualities inhering in the divine essence, not mere names, and God is not a being of absolute simplicity but infinitely complex.

The believer should not be anxious about bodily needs or hoard against future want, since with God no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for; but this trust does not excuse neglect of proper means and watchfulness.
The child can never perish who remains in the arms of an almighty Father, who will either not send trouble or give invincible courage to bear it.
The continual remembrance of death is the foundation of religious perfection; by the presence of this memorial and by continually meditating on that object, we may more perfectly learn to die daily.
The defiler of an innocent woman is a destroyer responsible to God, to be shunned and cast out, and wealth or position must not screen him.
The earthly tabernacle and temple were patterns and shadows of the heavenly things, so the heavenly sanctuary must be understood by the pattern shown to Moses in the mount.
The example of Christ's voluntary humiliation and obedience, even to a law that could not bind him, teaches us to submit punctually to laws of divine appointment and to love humiliations.

The fear of hell, far from signifying a backward step in the history of the religious spirit, is a proof of its having rejected the morally indifferent point of view and of its having become sovereign in union with the ethical spirit.
The fullness of the Spirit is a covenant privilege to be sought, received by the yielded and emptied heart, and may be repeated as need recurs.
The greater perfection a soul aspires after, the more dependent it is upon Divine grace.

The historian must be faithful in every sense: in sympathy with the subject, able to distinguish original from derived elements, thoroughly acquainted with the material, conscious of the limits of historical knowledge, and truthful; every historical study is an ethical task.
The inebriate cannot be made to leave his besottedness until his physical sense of pleasure yields to a higher sense; then he turns from his cups.

The law of parsimony requires us to apply the conclusions of the cosmological, teleological and anthropological arguments to one Being, not many; to this one Being we ascribe infinity and perfection not because they are demonstrably his but because our mental constitution will not allow us to think otherwise.
The love of the world and its honors is a chain that keeps the soul from rising to the heavenly Jerusalem; only an ardent desire of heaven can raise us thither.
The mode of the triune existence is inscrutable, and no analogy from nature or mind furnishes a proper analogue, since none contains tripersonality.

The nation, as well as the Church, is a divine creation; the Bible insists on nationality as existing by divine appointment, and the Kingdom of God will include all nations as its provinces rather than abolish national distinctions.
The pains of sense are salutary if they wrench away false pleasurable beliefs and transplant the affections from sense to Soul.
The poet should not strive to pitch his music higher than Nature, for she needs no song and is too beautiful; striving to surpass her only tires the heart.

The preachers who gain mighty results for God are those who have prevailed in their pleadings with God ere venturing to plead with men; the mightiest in their closets are the mightiest in their pulpits.
The question with the Lord is not how much wealth a man has but how he came by it and what he will do with it; the more means, the more responsibility.

The rights of woman are unfairly discriminated against by civil law; Christian Science furnishes no precedent for such injustice, and a wronged wife should be allowed to collect wages, hold property, and own her children.
The secret of a sound body is a sound heart; we should live with holy indifference to life or death, wanting to live only to be a blessing to others.
The sin which one has made his bosom companion comes back to him at last with accelerated force; the dragon is at last stung to death by his own malice.
The soul should not be content to linger in the cheerless tomb while morning rays illumine the green lake and dewy glade.

The speaker arises each day through a mighty strength, the invocation of the Trinity, and summons all powers between himself and every evil, with Christ before, behind, in, beneath, above, on the right and on the left.
The symbolic parts of a vision do not turn real persons, God, Christ, angels, or the redeemed into emblems; forsaking this rule makes symbolic prophecy a chaos.

The true aim of spiritual endeavour begins with personal salvation but goes beyond it to complying with the exquisite Will of God and the universal raising of the consciousness of the whole world, accomplished in each individual spirit in an individual manner.
The understanding of God as ever-present and omnipotent enables parents to heal their children's complaints.
The war is a revelation of the deadly evil at work in human nature and civilization, and therefore calls for humble national confession of sins rather than the Pharisee's thanksgiving of superiority.
The wrong done another reacts most heavily against oneself; right adjusts the balance sooner or later, and one cannot benefit himself by injuring others.
There is needed neither art nor science for going to God, but only a heart resolutely determined to apply itself to nothing but Him, or for His sake, and to love Him only.

Those who humbly do their duty, pay their tithing, care for the poor and fatherless and widows, honor the priesthood, and pray in their families build a foundation the gates of hell cannot prevail against.
Three things are best for a chief: justice, peace, and an army; three things are worst for a chief: sloth, treachery, and evil counsel.
To neglect to save the body when means are at hand is wicked; how much sorer the guilt of leaving souls to perish while saying it is not convenient.

True religion is most often seen in its simplest and purest character among the poor of this world who are rich in faith; the poor man's cottage may be the palace of God, while riches, worldly consequence, and high connexions throw great hindrances in the way of religious profession.

Vernacular Irish literature is the most primitive and original among the literatures of Western Europe, and its importance as the earliest voice from the dawn of West European civilisation cannot be denied.
We brought nothing but knowledge to direct labor; knowing how to employ time rightly is the greatest wealth, benefiting wives, children, and neighbors.
We must abide like a poor miserable creature before the throne of Divine Mercy, stripped of all action and affection to creatures, indifferent to all things.

We must bear trials if not with joy, at least with perfect submission, and remain assured that God only seems to withdraw Himself from us that we may follow Him more earnestly and unite ourselves more closely to Him.
We must frequently raise our hearts to God during the day, casting our care upon Him with great confidence, saying, 'I am thine, save me.'
We must not answer temptations nor appear to hear the enemy; if he is noisy, we prostrate ourselves before God and remain at His feet.
We must not yield to sadness, but labor independently of the heart in aridity through holy abjection and humility, living joyously amid holy occupations.
We ought once for all heartily to put our whole trust in God and make a total surrender of ourselves to Him, secure that He will not deceive us.
